sentences.text: Dubreuillosaurus was a carnivorous megalosaurid theropod dinosaur, a member of the large predatory family Megalosauridae.

The only known species is Dubreuillosaurus valesdunensis, which was originally described as a species of Poekilopleuron but is now recognized as physically comparable to the dinosaur Eustreptospondylus.

The holotype — the specimen the species is based on — was a subadult individual estimated to be 5 meters long and weigh 250 kilograms, though the adult length remains uncertain but has been indicated to reach up to 9 meters.

Matthew Carrano identified a unique notch on the rear of the braincase between the basioccipital and the exoccipitals and opisthotic as a distinguishing feature, while the skull itself was unusually low and long, with a length three times greater than its height.

Although the known juvenile specimen lacks crests or horns, it is possible these structures developed as the animal matured, leading to ongoing debate about whether Dubreuillosaurus possessed such ornaments.
The Dubreuillosaurus holotype is exceptionally complete, rivaling only Eustreptospondylus in the number of preserved skeletal elements among megalosaurids.
The 2005 paper establishing the new genus included a detailed description of the postcranial skeleton, providing insight into the animal's body structure beyond the skull.
Dinosaur bones were first noticed in 1994 by the mayor of Conteville during land rehabilitation at the Pierre de Caen quarry, where André Dubreuil observed remains appearing during work.
Professional excavations did not begin until 1998, after the quarry face had already been disturbed by a bulldozer and collapsed rock had been spread over a considerable surface by an excavator.

Scientists salvaged approximately two thousand bone fragments ranging from one to ten centimeters in size after sifting through many cubic meters of rubble, leading Ronan Allain to name the find a new species of Poekilopleuron in 2002.
The fossils were found in sedimentary rocks deposited in coastal mangrove swamps along the east coast of the Armorican Massif.

The habitat suggests that Dubreuillosaurus may have hunted fish and other marine prey, a hypothesis initially proposed by Allain who described the animal as a fish eater influenced by fish remains found with a related species.
Despite living on an island, Dubreuillosaurus did not exhibit insular dwarfism; its small size is attributed to it being a subadult, unlike the adult Eustreptospondylus found in similar settings.
Dubreuillosaurus valesdunensis was assigned to Megalosauridae in 2002, confirming its place within the family of large Jurassic predators.

In 2012, Carrano and colleagues placed Dubreuillosaurus in the Afrovenatorinae subfamily as the sister species of Magnosaurus, refining its classification within the parent group Eustreptospondylinae.
Dubreuillosaurus lived approximately 160 million years ago during the Bathonian stage of the Middle Jurassic, specifically from 168.2 to 165.3 million years ago.
During the Middle Jurassic, much of Europe consisted of a series of islands, creating a unique environment for these dinosaurs.
A 2024 study by Cau questioned the validity of Dubreuillosaurus, suggesting it is a junior synonym of Poekilopleuron due to individual variation.
